content: Naegele's Rule is a widely used method for estimating the expected due date (EDD) of a pregnancy. It is named after Franz Karl Naegele, a German obstetrician who developed this rule. Franz Karl Naegele was born on July 12, 1778, in Düsseldorf, Germany. In 1806, he became a professor and director of the lying-in hospital in Heidelberg. His textbook for midwives, Lehrbuch der Geburtshülfe, published in 1830, was highly successful and went through 14 editions. The rule calculates the EDD by taking the first day of the woman's last menstrual period (LMP), adding one year, subtracting three months, and then adding seven days. This calculation approximates the average duration of a normal human pregnancy, which is 40 weeks (280 days) from the LMP or 38 weeks (266 days) from the date of fertilization. For example, if the LMP was May 8, 2007, adding one year gives May 8, 2008. Subtracting three months results in February 8, 2008, and adding seven days gives February 15, 2008. However, the precise 280-day calculation would yield February 12, 2008. This method provides a reasonable estimation of the due date but is based on several assumptions. It assumes a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and that ovulation and fertilization occur on day 14 of the cycle, which may not be true for all women. To address variations in the lengths of calendar months and individual menstrual cycles, alternative tools such as hand-operated pregnancy wheels or electronic pregnancy calculator programs can be used. Since Naegele's Rule relies on the LMP date, it can be inaccurate by a week or more. Therefore, it is recommended to use this rule to calculate a range of possible due dates and confirm the gestational age with an ultrasound, particularly in the first trimester. Since the 1970s, ultrasound technology has allowed for direct measurement of the size of the developing embryo, providing a more accurate estimation of gestational age. Ultrasound dating is most reliable when performed in the first trimester (the first 12 weeks of pregnancy), with a 95% error margin of ±6 days. Scans conducted in the second trimester have an error margin of ±8 days, while those in the third trimester have a margin of ±2 weeks. In clinical practice, most obstetric departments in countries such as Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States use a combination of LMP-based and ultrasound-based estimates to determine the EDD. They often apply a 7-day or 10-day rule, meaning that if the LMP-based and ultrasound-based dates are within 7 or 10 days of each other, the LMP date is accepted as the EDD.
